title: State what improvement would look like
outcome: Write a testable claim about patient understanding and the cost of the change.
context: The clinic team has a prototype with a receipt-backed message and a delayed check-in branch.
teach: A design hypothesis connects a change to an expected behavior. Name the person, the task, the proposed change, and the observation that would support it. For this clinic, the change is a receipt-backed status. The expected behavior is that patients can explain whether the clinic received their arrival and choose the right next step.

State the mechanism. A message tied to the service receipt gives Mira evidence about what happened, while a sending state explains the interval before the receipt. The team expects these cues to reduce repeat check-ins and status questions. The explanation makes the claim specific enough to test.

Add a plausible cost. A longer message might slow people during a busy morning; a delayed state might send more patients to reception. Choose observations for both the intended benefit and the cost. Record what patients say the clinic knows, what they do next, and how long the task takes.

A useful hypothesis can change after study. Write an observation that would challenge the proposed mechanism, such as patients continuing to ask reception after correctly reading the receipt message. That result would direct the team toward lobby expectations or staff visibility.
keyDistinction: A testable hypothesis names an observable benefit, a possible cost, and the behavior that could change the team's view.
workedExample: The team writes: 'For patients arriving at the clinic, a message shown after the service receipt will help them identify confirmed check-in and move to the waiting area. The extra text may add reading time.' They prepare observations for status understanding, repeat entry, reception questions, and reading time. Each observation speaks to a part of the claim.
guidedQuestion: Which hypothesis gives the study the clearest observations?

options.label: A better confirmation screen will improve patient confidence and trust.
options.feedback: Confidence and trust matter. Name the exact message change, the patient action, and the observable sign of understanding to guide the study.

options.label: Receipt-backed wording will help arriving patients identify confirmed check-in and move to waiting, while its reading time may increase.
options.feedback: This names the change, task, expected behavior, and a possible cost. The study can observe understanding, movement, questions, and time.

options.label: The receipt message will reduce all reception questions and make the staff queue faster.
options.feedback: The message may influence questions. Queue speed comes from a separate service process, so test patient behavior and queue timing as distinct outcomes.

evidenceShift: Patients who understand the receipt and still seek staff help would shift attention toward the lobby journey and reception expectations.
transferContext: The prototype also includes a delayed state with a visible reception-help route.
transferTask: Write a second hypothesis about the delayed state. Include the expected patient action, a possible extra demand on reception, and an observation for each.
evidencePacket: Fictional proposed change: the kiosk shows a received message only after an appointment-service receipt.
Fictional proposed change: a delayed branch explains the request's current state and gives reception help.
Fictional current behavior: some patients repeat entry or ask staff after seeing Done.
artifact: Two testable hypotheses with observable benefits, costs, and challenging evidence.
assessmentFocus: Each claim connects a specific design change to a patient behavior and a realistic tradeoff.
assessmentCriteria: The change and patient task are named.
At least one observation covers the intended effect.
At least one observation covers a possible cost.

title: Write tasks that reveal understanding
outcome: Plan a formative study whose tasks and observations answer the clinic's decision.
context: The team needs to see how patients use the revised kiosk during confirmed and delayed check-in.
teach: A formative usability study observes people carrying out realistic tasks while a design can still change. Begin with the decision: does the revised flow help patients understand check-in status and move to the right next step? Recruit people who reflect the clinic's patients and the access conditions the team identified.

A task prompt gives the person a goal and a starting situation. 'You have arrived for your appointment. Let the clinic know you are here and show what you would do next' leaves room for a patient to choose an available route. The researcher can then observe whether the kiosk, signs, and reception route make sense together.

Define success in observable terms. The patient completes a check-in through a usable route, explains the receipt or delayed status accurately, and chooses a fitting next action. Record hesitations, repeated entry, staff requests, and privacy behavior. Use a consistent script for the prototype's receipt and delay branches.

Plan the study's boundary. A scripted prototype can reveal interpretation and task behavior. A connected service check can establish live receipt timing. Document the participants and setting so the team can interpret findings within the conditions that produced them.
keyDistinction: A believable task and an observable completion rule make a usability study actionable.
workedExample: The moderator gives Mira an appointment card and says, 'You have arrived for your appointment. Let the clinic know you are here, then show what you would do while waiting.' The facilitator triggers a delayed service response for one round. The observer notes Mira's route, her explanation of the status, and her next action. Afterward the moderator asks what she believed the clinic had received.
guidedQuestion: Which task prompt best reveals whether the clinic's full check-in route works?

options.label: Tap Check in, enter the code, and read the confirmation message aloud.
options.feedback: This checks a directed kiosk sequence. A goal-based prompt would also reveal how the patient finds the route and what they do after the message.

options.label: You have arrived for your appointment. Let the clinic know you are here, then show what you would do while waiting.
options.feedback: This gives a realistic goal and allows the available routes to emerge. Observe the status interpretation and the next action in each branch.

options.label: Look around the lobby and tell us whether the kiosk seems easy to use.
options.feedback: This can start a useful conversation about first impressions. Add an arrival task to observe actual completion and recovery behavior.

evidenceShift: A study focused on a specific physical reach issue would use a directed control task alongside the full arrival task.
transferContext: The team plans a round with a patient who uses a screen reader and a round during a noisy morning period.
transferTask: Add the participants, setting, and one observation to the test plan for each round. Keep the patient goal and completion rule consistent.
evidencePacket: Fictional research question: can patients distinguish received from delayed check-in?
Fictional prototype: the receipt and delayed branches use a facilitator script.
Fictional setting: the lobby includes glare, announcements, a kiosk, and reception staff.
artifact: A one-page study plan with participants, task prompts, branch script, observations, and completion rule.
assessmentFocus: The tasks represent the patient goal and the observations answer the decision question.
assessmentCriteria: The prompt gives a goal and starting context.
Success can be observed in the prototype.
The plan includes relevant access conditions and study limits.

title: Turn observations into findings
outcome: Report what happened, why it matters, and what explanation needs checking.
context: The team runs six fictional prototype sessions and compares patient actions with facilitator and staff notes.
teach: A finding begins with an observation from a stated task and setting. It then explains the consequence for the person and offers a possible cause as an interpretation. Keeping these parts distinct lets a team act on the evidence while leaving room for another explanation.

Read the session notes across participants before choosing a single example. Look for a repeated behavior, a serious one-off barrier, and cases that challenge the pattern. A six-person study gives the team direct evidence of those six sessions and useful signals for revision. The team can use broader service data to estimate how often a behavior occurs in routine operation.

Severity comes from the consequence, recovery effort, and conditions in which the issue appears. A patient who treats a delayed request as confirmed may wait in the wrong state. Another patient may reach reception and resolve it quickly. Both observations help the team choose the urgency and shape of the change.

Write each finding as a short chain: task and condition, observed action, consequence, interpretation, and next check. Link it to a design decision. A clear finding helps colleagues discuss the service behavior instead of debating a single quote.
keyDistinction: The count from a small qualitative study describes its sessions; service-wide frequency calls for broader measurement.
workedExample: In the fictional round, two of six patients read the delayed screen and moved to the waiting area as though check-in were complete. One asked reception for help, and three waited at the kiosk. The team records the two observed interpretations and the risk of an unrecorded arrival. It then checks whether the wording, visual hierarchy, or lobby signs led to that understanding.
guidedQuestion: Which finding best reflects the supplied six-session packet?

options.label: The delayed message causes patients to miss appointments, so the clinic should remove it.
options.feedback: The observed interpretation raises an important risk. Add the actual session events and a check of the message and service state before choosing a change.

options.label: Two of six patients treated the delayed screen as completion; the team should inspect wording and next-step cues before revising it.
options.feedback: This reports the observed sample and links it to a specific inquiry. Add the consequence for patients whose arrival still needs confirmation.

options.label: During the scripted delay, two patients moved to waiting before receipt; this could leave arrival unresolved, so test a clearer pending action and inspect lobby cues.
options.feedback: This connects the condition, observation, consequence, and next check. Keep the candidate explanation open while the team examines the message and setting.

evidenceShift: A video showing that the patients followed a lobby sign would give the setting a larger role in the next revision.
transferContext: In the same study, one patient uses reception after reading the received message because the entrance sign asks arriving patients to tell staff.
transferTask: Write a second finding card for this event. Give the observation, consequence, possible explanations, and a check that could separate them.
evidencePacket: Fictional study: six patients complete a scripted prototype check-in.
Fictional observation: during a delayed branch, two patients move to waiting, one asks reception, and three stay at the kiosk.
Fictional observation: one patient reads a received message and still visits reception after seeing the entrance sign.
Fictional system condition: a delayed branch has yet to receive a service receipt.
artifact: Two finding cards with observation, consequence, interpretation, and next check.
assessmentFocus: The findings describe the supplied sessions accurately and keep possible causes open for investigation.
assessmentCriteria: Each card names task and condition.
Counts refer to the fictional study sample.
The next check could shift the team's interpretation.

title: Revise, then test the change
outcome: Connect a design change to a finding and examine its new tradeoff.
context: Two patients in the fictional study treated a delayed check-in as a completed arrival.
teach: A revision proposes a mechanism for improving an observed experience. Begin with the finding: during a delayed branch, two patients moved to waiting before the service issued a receipt. Then name a change that helps patients recognize the pending state and choose a useful next action.

Change the smallest set of elements that can address the mechanism. The team can place a clear pending heading, explain that the request is still sending, and offer a reception-help action after a defined wait. The received state can keep its own distinct heading and waiting instruction. The contrast between states helps patients form an accurate expectation.

Retest the original situation and a routine successful check-in. The delayed task shows whether patients understand the pending action. The successful task shows whether the extra distinction adds reading time or confusion during normal use. Record understanding, next action, recovery, and task time.

A revision can expose a new question. Patients may understand the pending message and still need a clearer reception route. The next round turns that observation into another focused change. Iteration keeps the service aligned with actual patient behavior.
keyDistinction: A revision gains strength when its intended effect and its possible cost are both observed in the next test.
workedExample: The team changes 'Almost done' to 'Check-in is still sending' and adds 'Please stay here. Reception can help after one minute.' They keep 'The clinic has received your check-in' for the receipt state. In the retest, the moderator triggers both branches. The observer records whether patients distinguish them, where they go next, and how the extra wording affects a routine arrival.
guidedQuestion: Which revision and retest best follows the delayed-state finding?

options.label: Add a stronger pending heading and next action, then test delayed and received branches with the same arrival task.
options.feedback: This targets the observed interpretation and checks the new wording across both states. Include task time and reception use to watch for a new cost.

options.label: Add a confirmation dialog before every patient leaves the kiosk and compare completion time.
options.feedback: A confirmation could make departure more deliberate. Also observe whether patients understand the actual service state and whether the dialog affects routine arrivals.

options.label: Move the waiting instruction to a larger card and ask patients which layout they prefer.
options.feedback: The larger card may improve visibility. Pair preference with task observation so the team learns when patients believe their arrival is confirmed.

evidenceShift: Patients who understand the pending wording and still move to waiting would make lobby directions and reception practices the next focus.
transferContext: A patient sees the revised pending message during a busy session and chooses the reception-help route.
transferTask: Write one retest observation for this route and one service check that reception must complete to support it.
evidencePacket: Fictional original finding: two of six patients moved to waiting during a delayed branch before a service receipt.
Fictional proposed change: distinct pending and received headings with different next actions.
Fictional operations detail: reception can query the appointment service directly.
artifact: A findings-to-change table with revised copy, test tasks, observations, and a next decision rule.
assessmentFocus: The revision addresses a specific observation and the retest examines both understanding and added effort.
assessmentCriteria: Each change links to a finding.
The retest includes delayed and routine branches.
The next decision rule follows observable patient behavior.
